extracted.intended_audience: reformers, policymakers, landlords, philanthropists and general readers interested in urban housing reform and tenement management
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, design, management, financial and legal standards for building, operating, and evaluating model tenements in late-19th-century New York, with supporting statistics. Covers architecture, tenant amenities, management practices, profitability benchmarks and municipal regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair play between landlord and tenant
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair play between landlord and tenant is the key to unlocking success in improving tenement conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that equitable relationships are essential and that charitable giving alone is insufficient; sustained, fair treatment by landlords underpins lasting improvement (example: Miss Collins and Gotham Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal interest and active management by owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal interest in tenants and active, hands-on management by owners must form a large share of the capital invested for full returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners who personally look after tenants (time and effort beyond financial contributions) produce more durable improvements; landlords who tire or sell before completion often see relapse of conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent management and scale as success factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Model tenement enterprises succeed when planned on a sufficiently large scale and run with intelligent management and expert superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger planned blocks reduce per-unit cost of expert supervision and facilitate successful management (cited examples: Improved Dwellings Association, Tenement-house Building Company all declared 'eminently successful').

rubrics_metrics.name: Apartment size and outer rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Families should be provided with from two to four rooms, and rooms should be 'outer' rooms (i.e., each room should look out onto street or yard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Improved Dwellings Association houses supplied 2–4 outer rooms per family; the plan emphasizes sunlight and air by ensuring every room looks out upon street or yard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential tenant amenities and building features
rubrics_metrics.description: Model tenements should include functional amenities: coal lifts, ash-chutes, common laundries, free baths, individual sculleries and ash-flues, external fire-proof stairs, private front-doors, roof drying racks, and playground/park space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features reduce institutional character and improve tenants' daily life; A. T. White's Brooklyn plan is given as an exemplar embedding these features (play-ground, brass-band concerts, drying racks on roof, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcrowded narrow-lot designs (architectural limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impracticable to secure physical and moral health for 16–20 families on a standard narrow lot (e.g., 25 × 100 feet); plans should provide central yards or courts to supply air and sunlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee verdict cited: 'impossible to secure the requirements of physical and moral health within these narrow and arbitrary limits.' Larger blocks around a central yard are preferred for air/sunlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended building concentration and household-per-floor rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary practice favors concentration: four families per floor and twenty in the house as a common rule; increased crowding amplifies the need for guided planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The drift toward concentration eases management and supports economies of scale; larger-scale planning improves the promise of success versus many small houses on separate lots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert superintendence as first condition of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert superintendence is the first condition of successful management, and its cost is reduced in larger buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that professional on-site management is essential and that per-unit supervision cost decreases with building scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial governance: dividend limits and reinvestment
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate terms limiting dividends (example: limited to five percent on stock) with surplus reinvested in building maintenance and improvements are a recommended governance practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improved Dwellings Association limited dividends to 5%; dividends were paid and all surplus expended on buildings (new roofs, painting, fire-escapes, other improvements). This governance helped the experiment be 'eminently successful and satisfactory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Profitability benchmarks for model tenements
rubrics_metrics.description: Model tenements can be financially viable with modest returns — typically around five to six percent net — and even returns of 5–5.5% are reported as successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cherry Street houses returned 5–5.5% in three years; author asserts that owners should be content with 5–6% returns compared with safer investments with lower yields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenant profit-sharing / rent-insurance schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans that share profits with tenants (e.g., rent-insurance or dividend schemes crediting tenants with earnings above a threshold) are proposed to encourage promptness and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a proposed plan to credit tenant accounts with earnings above 4% was not yet carried out; A. T. White averaged nearly one month's rent back as a premium for promptness and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on liquor saloons and premises uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting liquor saloons on tenement premises is a moral/management policy that can reduce rental income potential but is considered desirable by model operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improved Dwellings Association forbade selling liquor on premises; the text notes saloons can fetch higher rent than ordinary stores but the Association still forbade them and invested surplus in tenant comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal/building regulations: lot coverage and open-space requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Corner tenements may cover the entire lot except 4 feet at the rear; tenements in a block may cover only 78% of the lot and must leave a rear yard 10 feet wide and air-shafts or open courts equal to 12% of the lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as legal/regulatory constraints that govern tenement footprints and mandated open space for ventilation and light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal/building regulations: height limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenements or apartment houses must not be built over 70 feet high on streets 60 feet wide, and must not be built over 80 feet high on streets wider than 60 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear numeric height caps are given as part of the building regulations excerpted in the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal definition of 'tenement' (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory/official definitions changed: in 1869 a tenement was a house occupied by four families or more; in 1888 a tenement was a house occupied by three families or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnotes clarify how the legal/administrative definition of 'tenement' changed over time, affecting counts and regulation applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of demographic and health statistics as evaluative metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Population density, persons per dwelling, death-rates, numbers of deaths in tenements, child mortality, and numbers of sick poor are used as indicators of tenement conditions and public-health impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appendix supplies many metrics (population by year/area, density per acre/square mile, death-rates for cities and tenements, child mortality spikes in houses with 60–80 tenants). These figures are presented as evidence to evaluate conditions and reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacancy rates and tenant order as success indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Low vacancy rates and minimal trouble with disorderly tenants are presented as operational metrics of a successful model tenement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Improved Dwellings Association block had rooms for 218 families with only nine vacant at one visit; Tenement-house Building Company had only four vacant of 106 apartments and reported the tenements 'a decided success.'
